summary: Describes the IETF's wishes for the rights that the IETF Trust should grant on IETF contributions, including Internet-Drafts and RFCs. Contributors grant rights to the IETF, and the Trustees manage them, including licenses to copy and implement, following direction from the IETF.

plainLanguage.summary: When an engineer writes an RFC, they keep their copyright but give the IETF Trust permission to pass the work on. This document is the IETF's instruction to the Trust about what that permission should let people do: copy a whole RFC, quote a passage, and take the computer-readable parts, such as grammar rules and schema files, and change them to suit their own software. It also says where the line is, which is that the running text of an RFC is not licensed for modification.

questions: what rights does the ietf trust grant
can i copy code from an rfc
subtitle: What the IETF wants the IETF Trust to let people do with the text and code in its documents.

tldr.problem: Contributors hand their copyright to the IETF Trust, and the Trust decides what rights to pass on to everyone else. The IETF wanted to say what those rights should be, but earlier attempts at writing the licence wording into the RFCs themselves had to be revised whenever a legal problem was found.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC states the IETF's wishes as guidance to the Trustees: copy RFCs freely, quote from them freely, extract and modify the code components, and do not grant rights to alter the running text.
tldr.outcome: It is an Informational document that supersedes RFC 5377. It deliberately does not supply legal wording, leaving the choice and upkeep of that text to the Trustees.

today: RFC 8721 was published in February 2020 as an Informational document and supersedes RFC 5377, the earlier advice to the Trustees. It has not been obsoleted or updated since. The document sets out the IETF's wishes rather than the licence wording itself, and it says the Trust remains the body that decides the exact wording and when changes take effect.

sections.title: Who Holds the Rights and Who Decides
sections.content:
Under the current operational and administrative structures, IETF intellectual property rights are vested in the IETF Trust, administered by a board of trustees. This includes the right to make use of IETF Contributions, as granted by contributors under the rules laid out in RFC 5378. The Trustees of the IETF Trust are therefore responsible for defining the rights to copy granted by the IETF to people who wish to make use of the material in these documents. The document uses the same terminology and the same meanings as RFC 5378.

The IETF Trust has indicated that it will respect the wishes of the IETF about what the granted rights ought to be, and it is therefore the IETF's responsibility to articulate those wishes. This document represents the wishes of the IETF regarding the rights granted to all users in regard to IETF Contributions, until it is superseded.

The RFC explains that the direction of the rights matters. The recommendations for outgoing rights are structured around the assumptions documented in RFC 5378: this document is about granting rights derived from those granted to the IETF Trust, and how those granted rights should in turn be passed on to others using IETF documents in ways and for purposes that fit with the goals of the IETF. The discussion is separate from the rights the IETF itself requires in documents to do its job, because those are not outbound rights, and it is expected that the rights granted to the IETF will be a superset of those copying rights the IETF wishes to grant to others.
sections.plainLanguage: There are two steps. First, the author gives the Trust permission to pass the work on. Second, the Trust passes rights on to everyone else. This document is about the second step, and about the limits the IETF wants the Trust to keep in mind when making it.

sections.title: Why These Rights Are Granted
sections.content:
The mission of the IETF is to produce documents that make the Internet work better. An important subclass of RFCs is standards describing protocols, and for these the primary value to the Internet is the ability of implementors to build solutions, whether products or software, that interoperate using these standards. The IETF therefore has a strong interest in seeing accurate, interoperable implementations of the material it publishes, and the IETF Trust grants rights to copy to people who make use of the text in RFCs in order to encourage exactly that.

As early implementations drawn from Internet-Drafts make use of descriptions in those drafts, similar desires apply to Internet-Drafts. The same considerations apply to non-standard, non-protocol documents such as Best Current Practice and Informational documents, and in this document the RFC recommends a common approach to the issue of right-to-use licences for all IETF documents.
sections.plainLanguage: The reason is interoperability. A standard is only useful if independent teams can build things that work together, and that requires them to be free to copy the text and to build on the machine-readable parts of it. The same reasoning applies to drafts and to documents that are not standards at all.

sections.title: Powers and Authority
sections.content:
The legal authority for determining and granting users rights to copy material in RFCs and other IETF Contributions rests with the Trustees of the IETF Trust, and this document provides guidance to that body, based on the rough consensus of the IETF. The Trustees have the authority and responsibility to determine the exact text insertions, or other mechanisms, needed in Internet-Drafts, RFCs and all IETF Contributions to meet these goals.

Earlier documents included the specific licence wording in the RFC text itself. The RFC says this has proved problematic: when problems are found with such text, even when the problem is not a change in intent, it is necessary to revise the RFC to fix the problem, and at best this delays fixing legal issues that need prompt attention. This document therefore describes the IETF's desires to the Trustees but does not provide the specific legal wording to address the goals, and the selection and updating as necessary of that wording is left to the Trustees. To ensure continuity, the starting point for licence text and other materials will be that previously created by the Trustees under the authority of RFC 5377, which this document supersedes. Changes to the IETF documentation and to document policies themselves take effect as determined by the Trustees.

One limit is stated plainly. The document does not specify what rights the IETF Trust receives from others in IETF Contributions, which is left to RFC 5378, and the Trust cannot grant rights it has not received. Likewise, the rights granted for pre-existing documents cannot be expanded unless the holders of rights in those contributions choose to grant expanded rights, although to the degree it can, without embarking on a massive effort, it is desirable if similar rights can be granted in older RFCs.
sections.plainLanguage: The Trust's lawyers write the actual licence wording; this document tells them what it should achieve. That separation exists because a wording mistake in an RFC can only be fixed by revising the RFC, which is slow, and the same mistake can be fixed in the licence policy without touching the document at all.

sections.title: Copying RFCs and Quoting from Contributions
sections.content:
It has long been IETF policy to encourage copying of RFCs in full, because this permits wide dissemination of the material without risking loss of context or meaning. The IETF wishes to continue to permit anyone to make full copies and translations of RFCs.

For quoting, there is rough consensus that it is useful to permit quoting without modification of excerpts from IETF Contributions. Such excerpts may be of any length and in any context, and translation of quotations is also to be permitted. All such quotations should be attributed properly to the IETF and to the IETF Contribution from which they are taken.

For the running text there is no consensus at this time to permit its use in contexts where the right to modify the text is required. The authors of IETF Contributions may be able and willing to grant such rights independently of the rights they have granted to the IETF by making the Contribution.

On additional licences, there have been contexts where the material in an IETF Contribution is also available under other licence terms, and the IETF wishes to be able to include content that is available under such licences, and it is desirable to indicate in the Contribution that other licences are available. It would be inappropriate and confusing if such additional licences restricted the rights the IETF intends to grant in the content of RFCs. The IETF does not wish to have contributions contain additional licences, because additional text in the document, and any additional licence referred to by permitted additional text, must not in any way restrict the rights the IETF intends to grant to others. Authors of contributions retain all rights in their contributions, so an author may grant any rights they wish separately from what the IETF grants, but a reader wishing to use such grants will need to consult external sources of information or contact the author directly.
sections.plainLanguage: Copying a whole RFC and translating it are both fine. Quoting a passage is fine, of any length, with the source named. What is not licensed is rewriting the prose of a specification: if you need to change it, you have to ask the author. A document may also point at another licence for the material, but only if that licence takes nothing away from what the IETF grants.

sections.title: Code Components
sections.content:
IETF Contributions often include components intended to be directly processed by a computer. These include ABNF definitions, XML Schemas, XML DTDs, XML RelaxNG definitions, tables of values, MIBs, ASN.1, and classical programming code. They are included for clarity and precision in specification, and it is clearly beneficial to permit their inclusion in products that implement the contribution.

Use of such code requires the ability to modify it. One common example is the need to adapt code for specific contexts such as languages, compilers and tool systems, which frequently requires some changes to the text of the code. Another example is that code included in open source products is frequently licensed to permit any and all of the code to be modified, and since the IETF wants this code included in such products, it follows that such modification must be permitted. While there has been discussion of restricting in some way the rights to make such modifications, the rough consensus of the IETF is that such restrictions are likely a bad idea and are certainly very complex to define.

The rough consensus is therefore that the IETF Trust is to grant rights such that code components of IETF Contributions can be extracted, modified, and used by anyone in any way desired. To enable the broadest possible extraction, modification and usage, the Trust should avoid adding software licence obligations beyond those already present in a contribution. The granted rights should allow creation of derived works outside the IETF that may carry additional licence obligations. As the Trust cannot grant rights it does not receive, these rights cannot be granted in contributions that are explicitly marked as not permitting derivative works.

Two mechanisms are suggested to document the intended grant to readers and users. The Trustees should maintain, in an easily accessible fashion, a list of common RFC components that will be considered to be code, starting with at least the items listed above and added to as they deem suitable or as directed by the IETF. And the Trustees should define a textual representation to be included in an IETF Contribution to indicate that a portion of the document is considered by the authors, later the working group and upon approval the IETF, to be code and thus subject to the permissions granted to use code.
sections.plainLanguage: Some parts of an RFC are meant to be run by a computer: the grammar rules, the schema files, the tables of numbers, the code samples. The Trust should let anyone take those, change them, and use them however they like, including inside products with their own licence terms. The Trust is also asked to keep a published list of what counts as code, and to define a marker that authors can put in a document to say that a section is code.

sections.title: IANA and the Security Note
sections.content:
No values are assigned in this document, no registries are created, and there is no action assigned to IANA. One list, of kinds of code sections, is anticipated, to be created and maintained by the Trustees of the IETF Trust, and it is up to the Trustees whether they create such a list and whether they choose to involve IANA in maintaining it.

The Security Considerations section says the document introduces no new security considerations. It is a process document about the IETF's intellectual property rights being granted to other people, and while there may be attacks against the integrity or effectiveness of the IETF processes, the document does not address such issues.
sections.plainLanguage: Nothing is registered with IANA here. The only list envisaged is the one of code section types, and the Trust decides whether to keep it and whether IANA should help. On security, the document simply says it is about process and not about security.

children.label: Inbound
children.note: Contributors grant rights to the IETF Trust, as set out in RFC 5378

children.label: Outbound
children.note: The IETF Trust grants rights to users. This document describes these

items.title: Reproduction of RFCs
items.text: Anyone may make full copies and translations of RFCs, so the material spreads without losing its context.

items.title: Quoting from Contributions
items.text: Excerpts of any length and in any context, without modification, with translation permitted and proper attribution to the IETF.

items.title: Using the running text
items.text: No consensus to permit use of RFC text where the right to modify it is required. Authors may grant that themselves.

items.title: Additional licences
items.text: Other licences may be named in a contribution, but they must not restrict the rights the IETF grants.
